title: Pars Plana Vitrectomy: Complications & Crisis Management
summary: A high-yield, comprehensive clinical guide to identifying, preventing, and managing the multi-phasic complications of pars plana vitrectomy (PPV). Essential for vitreoretinal fellows and residents mastering the surgical landscape.

sections.title: Clinical Overview & Taxonomy
sections.content: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) is the cornerstone of posterior segment surgery. While 23G, 25G, and 27G micro-incisional vitrectomy surgery (MIVS) has reduced trauma, complications remain significant. They are categorized by timing: Intraoperative (related to instrumentation and technique), Early Postoperative (<2 weeks), and Late Postoperative (>2 weeks).

branches: Scleral/Trocar: Subconjunctival gas, poor wound seal, uveal incarceration
Lens: Iatrogenic cataract (lens touch), phacofragmentation drop
Cornea: Epithelial edema (DM fold), Descemet's detachment
Vascular: Suprachoroidal hemorrhage (SCH), Retinal artery occlusion
Retina: Iatrogenic breaks (at trocar site or during traction relief)

rows: Severe pain, hypopyon, loss of Red Reflex
Aqueous suppressants (Timolol, Brimonidine); check gas volume
Intensive topical Pred Forte 1% or subconjunctival steroids
Suture leaky trocars, check for cyclodialysis cleft

sections.title: Late Complications: The Long-Term Burden
content: Cataract Progression: 80-100% of phakic patients require surgery within 2 years.
Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR): The leading cause of RD repair failure.
Epiretinal Membrane (ERM): Secondary to surgical trauma or residual hyaloid.
Neovascular Glaucoma: Especially in diabetic patients post-PPV.
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): Persistent inflammation or Irvine-Gass.
Silicone Oil Emulsification: 'Inverse hypopyon' and secondary glaucoma.

rows: Moderate: Inner retinal wrinkling, rolled edges of break
Severe: Full-thickness fixed retinal folds (CP: posterior, CA: anterior)

sections.title: The Endophthalmitis Protocol
content: Step 1: Clinical Suspicion (Pain out of proportion, AC cells/hypopyon).
Step 2: Immediate Vitreous/AC Tap (Gram stain, Culture & Sensitivity).
Step 3: Intravitreal Antibiotics (Vancomycin 1mg/0.1ml and Ceftazidime 2.25mg/0.1ml).
Step 4: Intensive Topical Antibiotics/Corticosteroids.
Step 5: Immediate Vitrectomy (EVS Trial: recommended if vision is Light Perception (LP)).

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: Sudden loss of Light Perception (LP) - rule out Central Retinal Artery Occlusion.
Increasing pain after post-op Day 1 - suspect Endophthalmitis.
Progressive vision loss with 'curtain' - suspect recurrent Detachment or PVR.
Hard eye on palpation - Acute Post-vitrectomy IOP spike (Gas expansion).

content.explanation: P: Pressure (IOP spike); O: Oil/Gas (Overfill or migration); P: PVR/Peeling trauma; S: Sepsis (Endophthalmitis).

sections.title: Landmark Studies in Vitreoretinal Complications
content: Silicone Study: Compared Silicone Oil vs. Sulfur Hexafluoride (SF6) for PVR. Oil was superior to SF6 for retinal reattachment.
EVS (Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study): Confirmed immediate PPV is beneficial for patients presenting with Light Perception (LP) vision or worse.
DRCR.net Protocol N: Evaluated PPV for DME; found it may be beneficial when vitreoretinal traction is present.

sections.title: Surgical Pearl: Avoiding Iatrogenic Breaks
content: 1. Angle Trocar Entry: 30-45 degree tunnel for better self-sealing.
2. Clear the Base: Use Chandelier lighting or indentation to view and clear the vitreous base.
3. Trim the Wound: Ensure no vitreous incarceration before removing trocars.
4. Check for 'Whisps': Use Triamcinolone Acetonide (Kenalog) to visualize residual hyaloid.
5. Low-Vacuum Entry: Approach the retina with caution using high-cut rate, low-vacuum settings.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform a 360° depressed fundus exam at the conclusion of every vitrectomy.
If IOP is high post-op with gas, check for pupillary block or expansion issues.
Pre-op prophylactic Aspirin usually doesn't need to be stopped for PPV, but Warfarin/DOACs require individual risk assessment.
Triamcinolone staining is your best friend for ensuring a complete posterior vitreous detachment (PVD).
